meta.title: Image Generation Workflows
meta.thesis: Image Generation Workflows becomes practical when you can map it to a decision, a workflow, and a validation check.

mentalMap.title: Image Generation Workflows: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Follow the path top to bottom: each step sets up the next.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: An image-generation workflow turns a prompt into pixels through a pipeline you can shape, validate, and rerun.

nodes.label: Mental model
nodes.orient: Start here: what a prompt-to-image workflow is and the problem it solves.
nodes.sub: Build the simplest useful picture of an image-generation workflow.
nodes.what: A mental model of prompt in, pixels out, with a pipeline in between.
nodes.relevance: It matters because every later choice only makes sense once you can picture the pipeline.

nodes.label: Mechanism
nodes.orient: How diffusion denoises in latent space to turn a prompt into an image.
nodes.sub: See the moving parts — encoder, latent space, denoiser, decoder.
nodes.what: The mechanism: text encoding, iterative denoising in latent space, then decode to pixels.
nodes.relevance: It matters because knowing where steps, guidance, and seeds act tells you what to tune.

nodes.label: Design choices
nodes.orient: The knobs that trade quality against speed, cost, and reproducibility.
nodes.sub: Choose model, steps, guidance, and seed to fit the job.
nodes.what: Design choices: the tradeoffs you set before running the pipeline.
nodes.relevance: It matters because the same prompt gives very different results depending on these settings.

nodes.label: Tiny implementation sketch
nodes.orient: A minimal runnable pipeline that turns one prompt into one image.
nodes.sub: Connect the concept to a small, real code artifact.
nodes.what: A tiny implementation: load a pipeline, pass a prompt and seed, get an image.
nodes.relevance: It matters because running the smallest version makes the abstract pipeline concrete.

nodes.label: Check and apply
nodes.orient: Last step: how workflows fail in practice and how to validate output.
nodes.sub: Use failure-mode awareness and a checklist to make it stick.
nodes.what: Check and apply: catch common failures and verify an image before trusting it.
nodes.relevance: It matters because a workflow you cannot validate is a workflow you cannot ship.

questions.prompt: When you first picture an image generation workflow in your head, what is the most accurate mental model?

options.text: A single button that converts text directly into a finished image with no intermediate steps.
A pipeline where a prompt is encoded, noise is iteratively refined by a model, and a decoder produces the final image.
A search engine that retrieves the closest matching photo from a database.
A painting program that fills in colors based on keyword tags.

questions.explanation: Image generation is a multi-stage pipeline — prompt encoding, iterative denoising, and decoding — not a single lookup or direct conversion.

questions.prompt: The core mechanism behind most modern image generators (like Stable Diffusion) is best described as:

options.text: Training a model to copy images pixel-by-pixel from a training set.
Gradually removing random noise from a noisy image, guided by a text signal, until a coherent image appears.
Combining two existing images using a weighted average.
Running a grammar checker on the prompt and mapping words to color palettes.

questions.explanation: Diffusion models work by learning to reverse a noise-adding process — they denoise step by step, steered by the text prompt at each step.

questions.prompt: When designing an image generation workflow, what is the central tradeoff you must manage?

options.text: File format (PNG vs. JPEG) vs. color depth.
Output image resolution vs. the number of words allowed in the prompt.
Image quality and control vs. speed and cost (more inference steps / larger models = better results but slower and more expensive).
Using a cloud API vs. storing images locally.

questions.explanation: The fundamental design tension is quality/control versus speed/cost — more denoising steps and bigger models improve output but increase latency and expense.

questions.prompt: You've written a minimal image generation script and run it for the first time. Name ONE concrete validation check you should perform to catch a realistic failure before trusting the output.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Any one of: visually inspect a sample of generated images for prompt-image alignment (does the output actually match what the prompt described); check that the output resolution matches the intended dimensions; verify the model loaded correctly by confirming a known simple prompt (e.g., 'a red circle') produces a recognizable result; log and inspect the seed so the output is reproducible; or confirm no NSFW / content-filter false-positives are silently returning blank images.
questions.explanation: A quick sanity check — such as testing a simple known prompt or visually auditing a small batch — catches silent failures like wrong model weights, misconfigured parameters, or content-filter blocks before they propagate.

questions.prompt: You're deciding how much rigor to apply to your image generation workflow. Which scenario correctly matches the RIGHT level of rigor to the situation?

options.text: Personal creative side-project → full production design with CI/CD pipelines, A/B testing, and cost dashboards.
Quick personal experiment → baseline (a single API call with a hardcoded prompt and default settings).
Customer-facing product generating thousands of images per day → baseline with no monitoring or error handling.
Advanced optimization → always the right choice regardless of scale or deadline.

questions.explanation: Matching rigor to context is the key 'check and apply' decision — a personal experiment only needs a baseline setup, while production scale demands proper design with monitoring, error handling, and cost controls.
